definitions.text: "Harold Ross … had a -for anything he did not understand which was practically everything."(Alexander Woollcott)

parts.words: "Harold Ross … had a -for anything he did not understand which was practically everything."(Alexander Woollcott)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: Woollcott said the New Yorker editor felt scorn for whatever he could not grasp, and the missing noun fills the dash

explanation.walkthrough: A literary fill-in-the-blank: supply the word from Woollcott's remark about Harold Ross, founding editor of The New Yorker.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names the disdain or scorn Ross felt for whatever baffled him.

clue.text: Isherwood claimed to be such an observer on Broadway

definitions.text: Isherwood claimed to be such an observer on Broadway

parts.words: Isherwood claimed to be such an observer on Broadway
parts.note: Isherwood's Berlin narrator says he is a passive recording device, and the stage version of his stories ran on Broadway under that title

explanation.walkthrough: Isherwood's Goodbye to Berlin opens 'I am a camera'; John Van Druten's play I Am a Camera (1951) took the line to Broadway.
explanation.definitionFit: Isherwood's narrator compares himself to a photographic device that records without judging.

clue.text: Solway saint is new, fashionable, and with Scottish name

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in 'the in thing'
Ian is the Scottish form of John

explanation.surface: A description of a Galloway saint as modern, trendy and bearing a Scots name.
explanation.walkthrough: St Ninian founded his church at Whithorn, on the Solway coast of south-west Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninian is the early missionary saint associated with Whithorn near the Solway Firth.

clue.text: Innovatively film Elena at home

indicators.note: doing something innovatively means doing it in a new way, so the letters of film Elena are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shoots a home movie of a woman called Elena in an inventive style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Innovatively' rearranges FILM ELENA into the French phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means within the family, privately among one's household.

clue.text: Cash cover for a Southern worker and lawyer in country knees-up (7, )

indicators.note: the cash word wraps round the rest, acting as a cover placed over the other pieces

parts.note: pence are small coins, i.e. cash
an ant is the classic worker in crosswords
DA is a District Attorney, an American lawyer

explanation.surface: A tale of money, a labourer and a lawyer at a rural party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover for' is the container signal: the cash goes round everything else. A knees-up is British slang for a lively party with dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustic folk dance is exactly a rural knees-up, a lively festive gathering.

clue.text: French provincial letter writer who understood the effects of pressure

definitions.text: who understood the effects of pressure

explanation.surface: A portrait of a French correspondent who grasped how pressure works.
explanation.walkthrough: Blaise Pascal wrote the Lettres provinciales, and Pascal's law describes how pressure is transmitted through a fluid.
explanation.definitionFit: Blaise Pascal wrote the Provincial Letters and formulated the physical law of fluid pressure, later honoured by the SI unit.

clue.text: Poetically pale, like bird ()

parts.note: as means like, in a comparison
a hen is a bird

explanation.surface: A poet's description of someone as white as a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashen describes a grey, drained complexion, a literary word for wan.

clue.text: Essayist supports company very quietly in production of ballet

indicators.note: in a down answer the supporting piece stands beneath the others, so it comes last

parts.note: pp (pianissimo) is the musical marking for very quietly
Elia was the pen name of the essayist Charles Lamb

explanation.surface: A writer backs a troupe performing a ballet very softly.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supports' puts ELIA beneath CO and PP. 'in production of' is link material.
explanation.definitionFit: Coppelia is Delibes's comic ballet about a lifelike mechanical doll.

clue.text: Seen as part of a golden host, it doesn't quite have the same ring

definitions.text: Seen as part of a golden host, it doesn't quite have the same ring

parts.words: Seen as part of a golden host, it doesn't quite have the same ring
parts.note: Wordsworth's 'host of golden daffodils' points to the flower; its old country name lacks the poetic sound of the familiar one

explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth saw 'a host, of golden daffodils'; the wild daffodil's folk name, from flowering in the spring fast, would not scan so well.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a traditional English name for the wild daffodil, which blooms around the season of fasting before Easter.

clue.text: Clausewitz, perhaps, remembered as jellyfish, or battleship

explanation.surface: Clausewitz is recalled as a stinging sea creature or an armoured vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: the Prussian strategist Clausewitz, the Portuguese stinging siphonophore, and an old sailing warship.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a soldier such as the strategist Clausewitz, the Portuguese stinging siphonophore, and an armed sailing warship.

clue.text: Feature containing short musical work for adoptive French pianist

indicators.note: containing means the facial word holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: the chin is a facial feature
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A composition is included in an article about a pianist who settled in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'containing' is the container signal. The Polish-born pianist made Paris his home, hence 'adoptive French'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Polish composer-pianist lived in Paris from 1831, so France was his adopted country.

clue.text: Unusual demands noted for Bonapartist conspirator

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of demands noted are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Strange requests are recorded by a plotter loyal to Napoleon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges DEMANDS NOTED. Dumas's Count of Monte Cristo is imprisoned after being denounced as a Bonapartist agent.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumas's hero is falsely accused of carrying a letter for the exiled Napoleon's supporters.

clue.text: One of the golden ones explored by Keats (and Margaret Drabble)? ()

definitions.text: One of the golden ones explored by Keats (and Margaret Drabble)?

parts.words: One of the golden ones explored by Keats (and Margaret Drabble)?
parts.note: Keats wrote 'Much have I travell'd in the ... of gold', and Drabble borrowed the phrase for a novel title

explanation.walkthrough: Keats's sonnet On First Looking into Chapman's Homer opens with travels in golden kingdoms; Drabble's 1975 novel is The Realms of Gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a kingdom or domain, the territory Keats imagines travelling through.

clue.text: Composer inadvertently causes landslide

indicators.note: something done inadvertently happens by accident, so the letters of landslide are jumbled

explanation.surface: A musician accidentally sets off a fall of rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inadvertently' rearranges LANDSLIDE; 'causes' is link material. Richard Addinsell wrote the Warsaw Concerto.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Addinsell was an English film composer, best known for the Warsaw Concerto.

clue.text: Constable landscape painting (of level crossing at factory?)

parts.note: flat means level
a ford is a river crossing
a mill is a factory

explanation.surface: A Constable picture is described as showing a level crossing beside a works.
explanation.walkthrough: Flatford Mill, on the River Stour in Suffolk, is the subject of several Constable paintings.
explanation.definitionFit: Constable painted the Suffolk watermill owned by his father many times, most famously in 1817.

clue.text: Higgins's "most original moralist in England"

parts.note: in Shaw's Pygmalion Professor Higgins gives this description of Eliza's father, the dustman

explanation.walkthrough: Higgins recommends Eliza's father, Alfred the dustman, to an American millionaire as England's most original moralist, which makes his fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Eliza's father, is the dustman whom Higgins praises in Shaw's play.

clue.text: Publicity suitable (with alternatives) for those modifying novels for television

parts.note: an ad is a piece of publicity
apt means suitable
or is the word introducing an alternative, so ors are alternatives

explanation.surface: Advertising is said to be fitting, with options, for TV adapters of books.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers who turn novels into scripts rework them for the screen, which is what adapting means.

clue.text: Academician as Greek god?

explanation.surface: A member of an academy is likened to an Olympian deity.
explanation.walkthrough: Members of the Académie française are traditionally called 'les immortels'.
explanation.definitionFit: French Academy members are nicknamed the undying ones, and Greek gods were deathless beings.

clue.text: Shipping house founded by Dickens (3)

parts.note: Dickens invented a London firm of shipping merchants that gives one of his novels its title

explanation.walkthrough: The novel's firm is a shipping house run by Paul Dombey, who longs for a male heir to carry it on.
explanation.definitionFit: This is both the name of the fictional merchant firm and the title of the Dickens novel about it.

clue.text: "Impatience of her chilly ceremony and annoyance at her want of ——" (Shirley, Charlotte Bronté)

definitions.text: "Impatience of her chilly ceremony and annoyance at her want of ——" (Shirley, Charlotte Bronté)

parts.words: "Impatience of her chilly ceremony and annoyance at her want of ——" (Shirley, Charlotte Bronté)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap from Charlotte Bronte's novel Shirley: supply the noun for self-assurance that the lady lacks

explanation.walkthrough: A literary fill-in-the-blank from Charlotte Bronte's Shirley.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means poise or self-possession, which a stiff, awkward hostess lacks.

clue.text: Samuel Taylor Coleridge as viewed by Thomas Love Peacock

definitions.text: Samuel Taylor Coleridge as viewed by Thomas Love Peacock

parts.words: Samuel Taylor Coleridge as viewed by Thomas Love Peacock
parts.note: Peacock's satire Nightmare Abbey caricatures Coleridge as a muddled transcendental philosopher

explanation.walkthrough: In Nightmare Abbey (1818), Peacock lampoons Coleridge as Mr Flosky.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Flosky is Peacock's comic portrait of the poet, his name taken from a Greek word for a lover of shadows.

clue.text: Provenance of Eliot's Phlebas ("a forthnight dead")

definitions.text: Provenance of Eliot's Phlebas ("a forthnight dead")

parts.words: Provenance of Eliot's Phlebas ("a forthnight dead")
parts.note: in The Waste Land, 'Death by Water' describes Phlebas, a drowned sailor, as a fortnight dead, and names his homeland

explanation.walkthrough: Eliot's 'Phlebas the Phoenician, a fortnight dead' appears in The Waste Land; the clue asks for his land of origin.
explanation.definitionFit: Phlebas is described as from the ancient seafaring Levantine land on the coast of modern Lebanon.

clue.text: Stephen King's time for a shift

definitions.text: Stephen King's time for a shift

parts.words: Stephen King's time for a shift
parts.note: Stephen King's short story collection is called ... Shift, so the time of day pairs with 'shift'

explanation.walkthrough: Night Shift (1978) is Stephen King's first short story collection.
explanation.definitionFit: The hours of darkness are the time for a late work shift, and King's collection pairs the two words.

clue.text: Urge on, partly to skimp electoral niceties (as at Eatanswill?)

indicators.note: partly means only part of the words skimp electoral is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A call to drive on while cutting corners in an election, as in Dickens's Eatanswill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' points to the run inside skIMP ELectoral. Eatanswill is the corrupt election town in Dickens's Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to drive or push someone forward, the sense of urging on.

clue.text: Spanish journalist also gets say in another form

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: 'Spanish journalist also gets say in another form' with no letter count. 'also gets say in another form' builds Y GASSET (Spanish y = and, plus an anagram of 'gets say'), the rest of Ortega y Gasset's name, not the letters ORTEGA, so no wordplay gives the answer.
annotationWithheld.clue: Spanish journalist also gets say in another form

clue.text: Victor Hugo, Diderot and Emile Zola are three such, familiar to Parisians

definitions.text: Victor Hugo, Diderot and Emile Zola are three such, familiar to Parisians

parts.words: Victor Hugo, Diderot and Emile Zola are three such, familiar to Parisians
parts.note: these writers' names are used for stops on the Paris Metro, which Parisians pass through daily

explanation.walkthrough: Victor Hugo, Diderot and Emile Zola are all names of Paris Metro stops, not just authors.
explanation.definitionFit: These are stops on the Paris underground railway, named after the writers.

clue.text: Possibly unlucky mark of respect from Patrick O'Brian?

definitions.text: Possibly unlucky mark of respect from Patrick O'Brian?

parts.words: Possibly unlucky mark of respect from Patrick O'Brian?
parts.note: O'Brian's naval novel The Thirteen-Gun ... has an unlucky number in its title, attached to a gesture of respect

explanation.walkthrough: Patrick O'Brian's Aubrey-Maturin novel The Thirteen-Gun Salute supplies the 'possibly unlucky' honour, thirteen being an unlucky number.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun salute is a ceremonial gesture of respect, and O'Brian's title gives one of thirteen guns.

clue.text: Yes, Lamb's disorientation in gathering

indicators.note: disorientation means the letters of yes and lamb's are thrown out of their order

explanation.surface: A confused lamb bleats agreement in the middle of a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorientation' rearranges YES and LAMBS, the S of the possessive counting as a letter here; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An assembly is a gathering of people for a shared purpose, such as a meeting.
